newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - True North sees steady results.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - True North sees steady results.

text.p: True North Communications Inc, parent of advertising agency Foote Cone & Belding, has moved through a transition period in which earnings sagged and is now headed towards stronger results, said Chairman Bruce Mason said in an interview.
The Chicago-based company's results, released earlier on Thursday and showing a 43.8 percent jump in the third quarter net profit, mark the start of the turnaround, Mason said.

The agency, the largest in the United States in terms of billings at $2.8 billion, suffered a bruising 1995 during which it lost the prestigious Colgate global ad account to New York rival Young & Rubicam and ended a promising international cooperation agreement with Publicis SA of France.
Since then, however, a string of major gains, most notably the $400 million SC Johnson account, have helped its outlook.

"This accelerated revenue momentum is projected to yield strong operating results for the full year," the company said in its earnings statement. But overall net profit is expected to decline from last year, Mason said.
"We always said that this would be a transition year," said Mason, adding that, after this year's dip, the year-on- year gains for the four years up to 1996 should resume.

"With the Colgate loss out of the way and S.C. Johnson kicking in, the results are going to turn higher for the rest of the year. And in '97, having the benefit of that (Johnson billings) all year, in general it looks like a good year for us."

The industry continues to be driven by a strong U.S. economy and growth in international marketing among the largest advertisers, Mason said. Global companies have sharply cut back on the number of agencies they deal with because "they want to maintain global brand integrity," he added.

IBM's Louis Gerstner grabbed the attention of the advertising industry two years ago when he gave all of Big Blue's advertising to WPP Plc, ending relationships with more than 20 other ad agencies around the world.
Mason said that was a critical event in the move toward global consolidation.
"The big beneficiaries of this consolidation are the biggest agencies," Mason said.
"That's why we've put so much into building our global infrastructure and in making technology investments. Now we feel we are good shape to service our gloal clients."
True North did not always exude such confidence about its global reach and there are still lingering worries about the failed relationship with Paris-based Publicis.
Publicis and True North remain partners in Europe, where a combined Foote Cone/Publicis venture has $3.2 billion in billings and is the largest agency in the region.
But the holding companies have given up any hope of patching up the alliance outside Europe and Publicis has begun to make acquisitions in markets that compete with its erstwhile global partner.

"They are building up their network to service their global clients and I wish them well," said Mason, who describes the ongoing Foote Cone/Publicis relationship as "parents who got divorced and still have joint custody of the child."
The joint venture "will be kept together because it's in our mutual best interest to keep it that way," Mason said.
He argued that, because of the nature of the joint venture agreement, "it's almost impossible to break it up."
Analysts watch the venture closely because it is one of the pillars of the agency's global network, so vital to winning international accounts.
Some doubts about True North's international clout were erased recently after it won big global account like S.C. Johnson, Tambrands and Kimberly-Clark.
"We have a global network that can go toe-to-toe with anybody," Mason said.
"The big global agencies are doing exceedingly well and that will continue. They have the overall growth of the industry, which looks good, but they also have the consolidation of global accounts."
